parts.note: read as the thing a bee is fond of: the sweet-scented climbing flower whose nectar bees seek out

explanation.surface: A two-word valentine from one insect to another.
explanation.definitionFit: Bees are drawn to this fragrant climbing plant for its nectar, so it is literally what a bee loves.

parts.note: read as small rodents with cheek pouches for storing food, not impudent ones

explanation.surface: Impudent small animals.
explanation.definitionFit: These small pet rodents carry food in large cheek pouches, so they are literally cheeky.

annotationWithheld.why: Cult-sharing performers in the Orient: NAUTCH GIRLS is an anagram of CULT-SHARING, but no word in the clue signals the anagram

parts.note: read as an Alpine singer breaking into falsetto, high notes among other things in a mountain song

explanation.surface: A singer who hits high notes among other accomplishments.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpine singers warble with sudden leaps into falsetto, producing high notes among lower ones.

parts.note: Neath looks like the Welsh town, but read as the poetic 'neath, short for beneath, it asks where something below lies

explanation.surface: Asking the way to a town in South Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: Neath is a town in South Wales; the answer treats it as the poetic contraction of beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: The poetic word 'neath is short for beneath, which means below.

parts.note: Prinny, the Prince Regent, built the oriental Brighton Pavilion; long before him Coleridge's Mongol emperor decreed a stately pleasure-dome in Xanadu

explanation.surface: An earlier architect whose work preceded the Prince Regent's.
explanation.walkthrough: Prinny was the nickname of George IV as Prince Regent, builder of the exotic Royal Pavilion at Brighton.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge's emperor who decreed a pleasure-dome in Xanadu built an oriental palace long before the Regent's Brighton one.

clue.text: Additional sod 'turned up for this part of the arch

parts.note: extra means additional

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the word sod is read from the bottom upwards

explanation.surface: Extra turf is dug up to build an arch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sod' looks like turf for building, but the indicator 'turned up' reads it upwards; an extrados is the outer curve of an arch.
explanation.definitionFit: The outer curved face of an arch is its extrados, the opposite of the inner intrados.

parts.note: Mr Bumble, the beadle in Dickens's Oliver Twist, declares that 'the law is a ...', so his verdict on the law is a donkey

explanation.surface: A rule named after a bumbling official or a bee.
explanation.definitionFit: In Oliver Twist the beadle Bumble says the law is a donkey, giving his famous ungrammatical verdict.

indicators.note: to appropriate is to take and adapt, so the word lab is taken and rearranged

explanation.surface: Asks what clothing is suitable in a laboratory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' reads as an adjective for lab clothing but rearranges LAB.
explanation.definitionFit: A white linen vestment worn by priests is an alb, a garment to wear.

clue.text: Richard Burton's rival keeps making a change

indicators.note: the letters of keeps undergo a change, signalling they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An explorer's rival keeps changing things around.
explanation.walkthrough: John Hanning Speke and Richard Burton, Victorian explorers, quarrelled over the source of the Nile; not the actor Richard Burton.
explanation.definitionFit: John Hanning Speke disputed with the explorer Burton over the source of the Nile.

clue.text: The shape of things to come

definitions.text: The shape of things to come

parts.words: The shape of things to come
parts.note: read literally: a hollow form that gives its shape to objects not yet cast, not H G Wells's futuristic novel

explanation.surface: The title of H G Wells's novel about the future.
explanation.definitionFit: A casting form holds the shape that later objects will take once poured, so it is the shape of things yet to be made.

clue.text: Contentious starter has to have a flat surface

parts.note: a deb (debutante) is a young woman starting out in society
a table is a piece of furniture with a flat top

explanation.surface: A quarrelsome beginner insists on having a level work surface.
explanation.walkthrough: A deb is a debutante, a young woman making her first appearance in fashionable society, hence a 'starter'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something open to argument is contentious, likely to provoke dispute.

definitions.meaning: a puzzling or tricky problem can be called a ...
something that tickles you, provoking laughter

explanation.definitionFit: A tricky problem is a tickler, and so is a feather or anything else used for tickling someone into laughter.

clue.text: A copper takes a little one' for a nudist

parts.note: an old penny was a copper coin, abbreviated d
a mite is a tiny creature or a small child

explanation.surface: A policeman arrests a small child for going about naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' is not a policeman: d stood for the old British penny, a copper coin. 'takes' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adamites were a sect who went naked in imitation of Adam before the Fall, so the word names a nudist.

clue.text: But are they, the flowers for nature morte!

definitions.text: But are they, the flowers for nature morte!

parts.words: But are they, the flowers for nature morte!
parts.note: nature morte is French for still life, literally dead nature; the clue asks if everlasting flowers can be dead

explanation.surface: Questions whether the blooms in a still-life painting are fit for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Immortelles are everlasting flowers, kept dried; their name means 'immortals', which seems at odds with 'dead nature'.
explanation.definitionFit: Everlasting flowers that keep their colour when dried bear a French name meaning undying ones.

clue.text: Where' an outside passenger finished up inside

definitions.text: Where' an outside passenger finished up inside

parts.words: Where' an outside passenger finished up inside
parts.note: recalls the limerick of the young lady who rode on a tiger and came back from the ride inside it, the town she came from

explanation.surface: A coach traveller riding on the roof ends up in the cabin.
explanation.walkthrough: The limerick: 'There was a young lady of Riga, Who rode with a smile on a tiger; They returned from the ride With the lady inside, And the smile on the face of the tiger.'
explanation.definitionFit: The limerick's heroine, who rode a tiger and ended up eaten, came from this Latvian capital.

parts.note: read as fungi with caps, which are picked by people gathering in the fields

explanation.surface: Headgear worn by farm workers bringing in the crops.
explanation.definitionFit: These fungi have caps and are gathered from meadows, so pickers in the field harvest the 'hats'.

clue.text: Inspiring, the work of Mr. Muscleman with his weights !

definitions.text: the work of Mr. Muscleman with his weights
definitions.meaning: a bodybuilder's activity of hoisting heavy weights off the ground

explanation.definitionFit: Something morally elevating is uplifting, and a weightlifter is literally raising his weights up.

clue.text: Disreputable lot might appear in deep rims

indicators.note: the letters of deep rims might reappear in a new order

explanation.surface: Shady characters could show up where pits have deep edges.
explanation.definitionFit: Demireps were women of doubtful reputation, a half-respectable set.

parts.note: in leapfrog the one bending over is told 'tuck in your tuppenny', tuppenny being slang for the head

explanation.surface: The leader of a group playing leapfrog.
explanation.walkthrough: From rhyming slang: twopenny loaf for loaf of bread, 'loaf' being slang for head.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang names the head after a cheap bread loaf, and leapfroggers are told to tuck it in.

definitions.meaning: a punishing ordeal that wears you out
read as making gruel, a thin porridge, with the verb ending -ling

explanation.definitionFit: A gruelling task is an exhausting ordeal, and the word also reads as preparing thin oatmeal.

clue.text: Youth's place in the bardic boat

definitions.text: Youth's place in the bardic boat

parts.words: Youth's place in the bardic boat
parts.note: Thomas Gray's poem The Bard has 'Youth on the ..., and Pleasure at the helm', placing Youth at the front of the vessel

explanation.surface: Asks where a young man sits in a poet's vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray's line sets Youth at the front of the gilded vessel, the bow of the ship.

clue.text: She certainly made a spectacular headstart

definitions.text: She certainly made a spectacular headstart

parts.words: She certainly made a spectacular headstart
parts.note: the Greek goddess of wisdom sprang fully armed from the head of Zeus, starting life out of a head

explanation.surface: Praise for a woman who got off to a flying start.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess of wisdom was born fully grown from the skull of Zeus.

parts.note: MA is Master of Arts
stiff means rigidly formal in manner

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster who is pompous yet fond of dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: MA is the abbreviation for Master of Arts. 'but' joins the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A large powerful guard dog breed is a mastiff, here called doggy as a thing of the canine kind.

clue.text: He gets taken out by a derider .

definitions.text: He gets taken out by a derider .

parts.words: He gets taken out by a derider .
parts.note: a mocker is said to be taking the mickey, so the person taken out is a man of that name

explanation.surface: A man is escorted out by someone who scorns him.
explanation.walkthrough: To take the mickey is British slang for to tease or mock someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone mocking is taking the mickey, so the fellow taken is named in the idiom.

clue.text: There's a new part to the old port

annotationWithheld.why: There's a new part to the old port: ANTWERP is an anagram of NEW PART, but the only anagram signal is 'new', which is also fodder; no other word signals the rearrangement
annotationWithheld.clue: There's a new part to the old port

parts.note: a means one

explanation.surface: Someone skilled in a single area of work.
explanation.definitionFit: An adept person is highly skilled.

definitions.meaning: a member of the religious order of Our Lady of Mount Carmel
the name of a variety of pear

explanation.definitionFit: A White Friar belongs to the Carmelite religious order, and Carmelite is also the name of a pear variety.

definitions.meaning: a liquor distilled from sugar cane
an island in the Inner Hebrides

explanation.definitionFit: Rum is old slang for odd, a cane liquor, and an Inner Hebridean island.

parts.note: in Scott's ballad Lochinvar the brave young knight carries off 'the fair ...' from her wedding

explanation.surface: Praise for a hero and the girl he loves.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's poem Marmion tells how young Lochinvar rode off with his sweetheart, the bride Ellen.

parts.note: murphy is slang for a potato, so this is the starchy tuber eaten in hot countries in place of it

explanation.surface: An Irishman named Murphy on holiday somewhere hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Murphy' is old British and Irish slang for a potato, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: This tropical tuber plays the potato's part in hot climates, a sweet starchy root vegetable.

clue.text: Performed in the manner of Samson Agonistes

definitions.text: Performed in the manner of Samson Agonistes

parts.words: Performed in the manner of Samson Agonistes
parts.note: Milton's Samson Agonistes is Samson after the Philistines put out his eyes, so anything done like him is done blind

explanation.surface: Stage directions for acting a part from Milton.
explanation.walkthrough: Samson Agonistes is Milton's verse drama about Samson, blinded and captive in Gaza.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's blinded Samson acts without eyesight, so in his manner means blindly.
